doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Studio demands, takes, headphones and click tracks
summary: College music was harder than studio work; sessions involved several takes, click tracks, and pre-recorded award shows.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How much of that skill required can you attribute to Fredonia and/or Eastman?

Oh everything. There’s nothing I saw — let me see if I can phrase this correctly — there is no music I saw in the professional world that was as difficult as I saw in college. It’s all easy after that. Because in college, you know, don’t forget, if you’re selling soap, they don’t want you listening to the music so it can’t be very difficult.
That’s a perfect way to put it. Yeah, sure.
Yeah. But yet it’s still challenging to you, to the player, to get it right the first time because you know, the contractor doesn’t want to go like that and go —
We have to take another take for that? Yeah.

We do do several takes. It’s not as instant as one may make it out. We do get to rehearse it, we do get to play it several times, and it’s pretty polished by the time we do it. Because we get called, it’s a 3-hour call, whether we’re there three minutes or three hours. The pay is the same. After three hours then it goes up. So they figure to have us, let’s get a half a dozen takes or more in the book.
Was most of it wearing headphones and playing to something that was already recorded?

Yeah. Most times the rhythm section was on track already so we were with phones, and played to the click-track it’s called. I mean we had click, and we also had drums, so if the drummer wore a click-track he’d be right with it so it didn’t matter which we listened to. Sometimes the click-track would be annoying because it’s just a click-click — it would be a metronome. So we’d ask to shut the click off and we’d play to drums. Yeah. And that’s most of it. Some of it was live. But they’d want to get it perfectly. So you know the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

way that a TV show, like an award show, which I did a lot of award shows, and you’d see the guy going to commercial and that’s a lot of pre-record, so we’re not even playing. Sometimes we are, but a lot of times it was pre-recorded so it’s perfect. They didn’t want instruments making mistakes on air.
